channel.title: Coding on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Coding on Best of AI

item.title: Claude Fable 5.1
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 on September 1, 2026, alongside Mythos 5.1, a restricted-access version of the same underlying model available to vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences organizations that need capabilities the public release keeps guarded. Fable 5.1 keeps the same $10 per million input and $50 per million output token pricing as Fable 5, but cuts prompt-cache reads from $1.00 to $0.25 per million tokens, a change Anthropic says lowers effective cost by around 25 percent for typical workloads and as much as 45 percent for heavily agentic ones that lean on cached context. Anthropic reported 52.6 percent on Terminal-Bench-Science as one of the headline benchmark gains over the original Fable 5.

item.title: Muse Spark 1.3
item.description: Meta shipped Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026, its biggest coding and agentic jump yet and, according to AI chief Alexandr Wang, a model that closes much of the gap with frontier releases like GPT-5.6. It cuts token usage by 25 percent and tool calls by 20 percent on comparable tasks, and holds the same $1.25 per million input and $4.25 per million output token pricing as its predecessor, plus a contributor tier at a steep discount for developers who let Meta train on their prompts and completions. Access starts through Muse Code and the Meta API, with a “max reasoning” variant still going through safety testing before release, and a rollout to Meta AI, Instagram, and Facebook planned to follow.

item.title: Aloud
item.description: Aloud is built for the gap between what a developer means and what ends up in a written bug report or feature request. It records voice, screen, and a live transcript while someone talks through their app the way they naturally would, pointing at elements and changing their mind mid-sentence, then converts that into a clean set of instructions, flags anything that could be read two ways, and attaches the relevant screenshots.

item.title: GitNexus
item.description: GitNexus turns a codebase into a knowledge graph that coding agents can query for exact structural information, such as which functions call a given piece of code or which services depend on an API, instead of relying on embedding-based search that can miss or misjudge relationships. It ships with agent skills for exploring, debugging, impact analysis, and refactoring, and can flag when a change in one repository will break something in another before that change is merged.

item.title: GLM-5.3-Flash
item.description: Zhipu AI officially revealed GLM-5.3-Flash on August 26, 2026, confirming it as the model previously seeded anonymously on testing platforms under the name “Ox Alpha,” which had drawn over 50 trillion tokens of traffic in five days before anyone knew who built it. It’s a 320-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 18 billion active parameters per token, the first natively multimodal release in the GLM-5 line, combining a hybrid sparse-and-linear attention design with a 1-million-token context window. Zhipu pretrained it on a 30-trillion-token multimodal corpus and says it matches Nvidia GPU-based models on efficiency and token cost while running on domestic Chinese chips.

item.title: Grok 4.6
item.description: xAI released Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, extending Grok 4.5’s coding focus toward longer-running agent sessions and more demanding interactive and visual tasks. The model carries a 500,000-token context window, accepts text and image input, and exposes configurable reasoning effort levels from low to xhigh so developers can trade off latency against depth on a given request. xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens for prompts under 200,000 tokens, with rates roughly doubling once a request crosses that threshold.

item.title: Gemini 3.7 Flash
item.description: Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash on August 13, 2026, just three weeks after 3.6 Flash, keeping the same 1,048,576 token input window and 65,536 token output ceiling while moving the knowledge cutoff to March 2026. Google credits the gains to developer feedback and algorithmic changes rather than a bigger model, and the benchmark jumps are large: DeepSWE v1.1 climbs from 49.0 to 65.3 percent, FrontierCode 1.1 Main goes from 34.4 to 43.6 percent, and Zapier’s AutomationBench nearly doubles from 17.0 to 30.4 percent. Input pricing is cut in half to $0.75 per million tokens as introductory pricing through the end of 2026.

item.title: GLM-5.3
item.description: Zhipu AI released GLM-5.3 on August 14, 2026, calling it the strongest open-weights coding model available, though the weights themselves are not landing until two weeks after the announcement. It shares its base architecture with GLM-5.2, so the roughly 50 percent jump in coding capability Zhipu reports comes entirely from extended post-training rather than a larger model. The company points to a security angle in particular: GLM-5.3 scored 84.5 percent on CyberGym, a benchmark for finding and validating vulnerabilities from source code, edging out Anthropic’s Claude Mythos at 83.8 percent and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol at 83.6 percent. Zhipu says internal security teams used the model to surface 2,436 vulnerabilities across 269 projects.

item.title: Gemini 3.6 Flash
item.description: Gemini 3.6 Flash replaced Gemini 3.5 Flash as Google’s default workhorse model on July 21, 2026, part of a three-model July drop that also included Flash-Lite and a restricted Flash Cyber variant, with Gemini 3.5 Pro still not shipped. It keeps the 1,048,576 token context window and 65,536 token output ceiling, moves the knowledge cutoff to March 2026, and uses about 17 percent fewer output tokens than its predecessor while scoring higher on coding, long-context, and computer-use benchmarks, including a jump from 37 to 49 percent on DeepSWE. Output pricing dropped from $9.00 to $7.50 per million tokens, with input still at $1.50 per million and cached input at $0.15 per million. Independent evaluations are more mixed than Google’s own numbers suggest: the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores it even with 3.5 Flash, and community coding tests put it behind GPT-5.6 Luna, Grok 4.5, and Kimi K3 on several tasks.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.5
item.description: Claude Opus 4.5 is the Opus-tier model Anthropic released on November 24, 2025, and its headline change was price: input tokens dropped to $5 per million and output to $25 per million, a two-thirds cut from Opus 4.1’s $15/$75 rate. It scored 80.9 percent on SWE-bench Verified at launch, ahead of Gemini 3 Pro’s 76.2 percent and GPT-5.1 Codex Max’s 77.9 percent on the same benchmark, and Anthropic added an “effort” parameter that lets developers dial reasoning depth up or down per request. It kept the 200,000 token context window and image input support from earlier Opus releases, and shipped alongside a round of Claude Code updates aimed at longer autonomous coding sessions. Anthropic followed it with Opus 4.6 in February 2026 and Opus 4.7 in April, each holding the same $5/$25 pricing while pushing coding scores further.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.7
item.description: Claude Opus 4.7, released April 16, 2026, is a direct upgrade to Opus 4.6 aimed at the hardest software engineering tasks, the ones where earlier Opus models still stumbled on large, unfamiliar codebases. Pricing held at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, and it kept the 1 million token context window with up to 128,000 tokens of output. It shipped with a new tokenizer that produces up to 35 percent more tokens for the same input text, a tradeoff Anthropic made to improve accuracy on code-heavy prompts. It’s available through claude.ai, the API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.

item.title: Claude Opus 5
item.description: Claude Opus 5 is Anthropic’s newest Opus-tier model, released July 24, 2026 at the same $5/$25 per million token pricing as Opus 4.8, half of what the larger Claude Fable 5 model charges for similar intelligence. It ships with a low, medium, and high effort toggle so developers can trade cost against reasoning depth on a per-request basis, plus a faster mode that doubles the price to $10/$50 in exchange for roughly 2.5 times the speed. On SWE-bench Pro it scored 79.2 percent, roughly double the agentic coding score Anthropic reported for the previous Opus generation, and it posted 43.3 percent on Frontier-Bench and 30.2 percent on ARC-AGI-3. It carries the 1 million token context window that has been standard across the Opus line since Opus 4.6, and it’s available on claude.ai, the API, and the major cloud platforms from launch.

item.title: DeepSeek V3.2
item.description: DeepSeek V3.2 is DeepSeek’s update to V3.1, publicly detailed on December 1, 2025 after an experimental preview in September. It introduces DeepSeek Sparse Attention, a fine-grained sparse attention mechanism that cuts training and inference cost while preserving quality on long-context tasks, and the flagship Speciale variant carries roughly 685 billion parameters in a mixture-of-experts layout. The context window sits at 163,840 tokens with up to 64,000 tokens of output, and DeepSeek reports gold-medal-level results on 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad and International Olympiad in Informatics problem sets. API pricing runs around $0.21 per million input tokens and $0.32 per million output tokens, roughly half of what V3.1-Terminus cost, particularly for long-context decoding. Like the rest of the DeepSeek lineup it ships under the MIT license with weights on Hugging Face, and it served as the base DeepSeek built V4-Pro on the following spring.

item.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash
item.description: Gemini 3.5 Flash launched at Google I/O on May 20, 2026 and immediately replaced Gemini 3 Flash as the default model in the Gemini app, Google Search’s AI Mode, and the Gemini API. It handles a 1,048,576 token input window with up to 65,536 tokens of output across text, image, audio, and video, and Google says it runs about four times faster than other frontier models while beating Gemini 3.1 Pro on several coding and agentic benchmarks, including 76.2 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Pricing is $1.50 per million input tokens and $9.00 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted 90 percent to $0.15 per million, and dynamic thinking is enabled by default rather than requiring a separate flag.

item.title: GLM-5
item.description: GLM-5 is Zhipu AI’s frontier open-weight model, released February 11, 2026 as roughly a two-times scale-up from GLM-4.5, growing from 355 billion to about 744 billion total parameters while keeping a similar 40 billion active per token in its mixture-of-experts design. It ships with a 203,000 token context window, well short of the 1 million tokens its GLM-5.2 successor would add four months later, and Zhipu trained it entirely on Huawei Ascend chips using the MindSpore framework rather than Nvidia hardware. API pricing starts at $0.57 per million input tokens and $1.92 per million output tokens through Zhipu’s own platform and the WaveSpeed API. It shipped under the MIT license, and coverage at the time framed it as the first frontier-class model from a Chinese lab built on fully domestic hardware.

item.title: MiniMax M2.5
item.description: MiniMax M2.5, released February 12, 2026, extends the coding-focused M2.1 model into general office work: generating and editing Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files and switching between different software environments within an agentic workflow. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 230 billion total parameters and 10 billion active per token, ships with a 204,800 token context window and up to 128,000 tokens of output, and comes in two variants, a standard mode running at roughly 50 tokens per second and a Lightning mode at double that speed. MiniMax prices API access at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.90 per million output tokens, among the cheapest rates of any frontier-class model at release, and it ships with open weights under a modified MIT license for self-hosting.

item.title: Mistral Large 4
item.description: Mistral Large 4 replaces Large 3 as Mistral AI’s proprietary flagship, roughly eight months after that model shipped in December 2025. It’s a 190 billion parameter dense model with a 256,000 token context window, priced at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens through Mistral’s own La Plateforme as well as Azure AI Foundry and AWS Bedrock. Mistral says the gains over Large 3 are concentrated in coding and multi-step reasoning, an area where the company has been trying to close the gap with GPT-5.6 and Claude Sonnet 5 rather than compete on raw scale.

item.title: Claude 3.5 Sonnet
item.description: Claude 3.5 Sonnet is a text-and-image language model from Anthropic, first released in June 2024 as a mid-tier upgrade to the Claude 3 lineup that matched or beat the larger Claude 3 Opus on most benchmarks while running faster and cheaper. Anthropic updated it again in October 2024 with a version that added computer use, a feature letting the model view a screenshot and control a mouse and keyboard to operate software the way a person would. That update made Claude 3.5 Sonnet one of the first widely available models built for agentic tasks like filling out web forms, navigating operating systems, and running multi-step workflows without a human clicking each button. It kept the 200,000 token context window of its predecessors and priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, positioning it as Anthropic’s workhorse model through much of 2024 and early 2025 before the Claude 3.7 and Claude 4 lines replaced it.

item.title: Claude Fable 5
item.description: Claude Fable 5 is a public, safety-restricted release of Mythos, an internal Anthropic model class that the company unveiled in April 2026 and initially withheld from general availability because of its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Anthropic made Fable 5 available to enterprise customers and paid subscribers on June 9, 2026, after adding safeguards that redirect queries in high-risk areas like cybersecurity and biology to Claude Opus 4.8 instead, a mechanism the company says triggers in under 5 percent of sessions. On paper it is the strongest model Anthropic has shipped publicly: 95.0 percent on SWE-bench Verified, 80.3 percent on the harder SWE-bench Pro, and 92.6 percent on GPQA Diamond, with strong results in vision and scientific research tasks as well. It carries a 1 million token context window and is priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, double what Anthropic charges for Opus 4.8, reflecting its positioning as a specialty top-tier option rather than a general daily driver.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 5
item.description: Claude Sonnet 5 launched on June 30, 2026 as Anthropic’s most agentic Sonnet model yet, built to plan multi-step tasks and use tools like browsers and terminals with less hand-holding than earlier Sonnet versions. It performs close to Claude Opus 4.8 on most benchmarks, including roughly 85.2 percent on SWE-bench Verified and 63.2 percent on SWE-bench Pro, while costing noticeably less, which is why Anthropic and reviewers have framed it as a cheaper way to run coding agents at scale. It carries a 1 million token context window with context compaction to manage long agent sessions, and reads both text and images. Anthropic priced it at an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through August 31, 2026, after which it moves to standard pricing of $3/$15, and it is now the default model for free and Pro Claude.ai plans.

item.title: DeepSeek V4-Pro
item.description: DeepSeek V4-Pro is DeepSeek’s flagship model, released on April 24, 2026 alongside a smaller sibling, V4-Flash. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 1.6 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active per token, and it introduces a hybrid attention design combining Compressed Sparse Attention and Heavily Compressed Attention that cuts inference compute and KV-cache size sharply compared to V3.2, letting it handle a 1-million-token context window. The model runs in both a “thinking” mode for step-by-step reasoning and a non-thinking mode for fast responses, and DeepSeek reports it leading open-weight models on math, science, and agentic coding benchmarks, with a SWE-bench Verified score above 80%.

item.title: GLM-5.2
item.description: GLM-5.2 is Zhipu AI’s flagship open-weight model, released on June 13, 2026 under the MIT license. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with roughly 744 billion total parameters and about 40 billion active per token, and it ships with a context window of 1 million tokens, far beyond the 128,000-token window of its GLM-4.6 predecessor. Zhipu built it specifically for long-horizon coding agents, training it for months on agentic software engineering scenarios rather than general chat.

item.title: GPT-4.1
item.description:
GPT-4.1 is OpenAI’s April 2025 model, released as an API-only update aimed squarely at developers rather than ChatGPT users. Its headline feature is a 1-million-token context window across all three variants, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 Mini, and GPT-4.1 Nano, an eightfold jump over GPT-4o’s 128,000 tokens. It scores 80.1% on MMLU and 54.6% on SWE-bench Verified, a 21-point improvement over GPT-4o on real-world software engineering tasks pulled from GitHub issues.

OpenAI priced the flagship variant at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens, about 26% cheaper than GPT-4o, while GPT-4.1 Mini undercuts GPT-4o by roughly 83% on many benchmarks. The combination of long context and coding performance made it popular quickly for tools that need to process large codebases or long documents in a single pass, and it effectively replaced GPT-4.5 as OpenAI’s recommended model for API use later in 2025.

item.title: Grok 4.5
item.description: Grok 4.5 is xAI’s model released on July 8, 2026, built with a heavier emphasis on coding, agentic workflows, and knowledge work than earlier Grok releases. On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scored 54, placing fourth overall among frontier models while taking the top spot specifically on agentic tool use, and it posted 83.3 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 64.7 percent on SWE-Bench Pro, both benchmarks aimed at real coding and terminal tasks rather than multiple-choice knowledge tests. It carries a 1-million-token context window and handles text and image input, and xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, with a cheaper $0.50 rate for cached input tokens. It’s reachable through the xAI API console, the Grok app, X, and a wide set of third-party integrations including Cursor, OpenRouter, Vercel, and Microsoft’s Word, Excel, and PowerPoint add-ins. Some coverage framed it as xAI’s answer to Anthropic’s Opus-class models, given the shared focus on long agentic coding sessions.

item.title: MiniMax M3
item.description: MiniMax M3 is an open-weight mixture-of-experts model that MiniMax released in June 2026, with weights on Hugging Face by June 7. It has around 428 billion total parameters with roughly 23 billion active per token, spread across 256 fine-grained experts, and MiniMax bills it as the first open-weight model to pair frontier-level coding ability with a 1 million token context window and native multimodal input across text, images, and video. The lab reports 59% on SWE-Bench Pro and 66% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, benchmarks aimed at long-running coding and agent tasks rather than one-off question answering.
